title: Inhaling CO2 Cleared Alzheimer's Proteins in Early Human Trial
excerpt: A 30-minute session of intermittent high-dose carbon dioxide inhalation flushed toxic proteins from the brain by mimicking deep-sleep cleansing mechanisms, while a separate copper-based drug showed similar promise in mice.
body:
• Intermittent inhalation of 5% CO2 for 30 minutes activated the brain's glymphatic waste-clearance system in 12 human participants, flushing out beta-amyloid and tau proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease.
  • A separate study found that a copper-delivering drug, Cu(ATSM), restored critical protein pumps in the blood-brain barrier, reducing toxic amyloid-beta by 42% and improving spatial learning by 44% in Alzheimer's-model mice.
  • Both approaches remain in early stages — the CO2 study had only 12 participants and the copper drug has only been tested in animals — but researchers say they open promising new avenues for treatment.

Two independent research teams have demonstrated novel methods for clearing toxic proteins from the brain that accumulate in Alzheimer's disease, offering new hope in the fight against a condition that affects more than 55 million people worldwide.

In the first study, presented last week at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference (AAIC) in London, researchers showed that intermittent inhalation of high-dose carbon dioxide could activate the brain's natural waste-removal system while participants were awake. In the second, published in ACS Chemical Neuroscience, a copper-delivering drug repaired damaged protein pumps in the blood-brain barrier of mice, dramatically reducing the toxic protein burden.

The CO2 Inhalation Breakthrough

Sephira Ryman, a researcher at the University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, led the CO2 study with 12 participants — eight with no signs of cognitive impairment and four with elevated levels of tau protein and mild cognitive decline. Each wore a mask that alternated between normal air (0.05% CO2) and air containing 5% CO2, switching every 35 seconds for half an hour.

The approach works by mimicking the brain's deep-sleep cleansing process. During deep sleep, slow brain waves cause blood vessels to rhythmically dilate and constrict about once every 30 seconds, driving the glymphatic system — a network of channels that flushes waste products from brain tissue.

"This dilation and constriction essentially serves as a pump that clears waste from the brain."

— Sephira Ryman, University of New Mexico

Blood samples taken 15 minutes after the session showed elevated levels of beta-amyloid in the blood of all participants, indicating the protein was being flushed from the brain. The intervention also appeared to boost clearance of tau protein, but only among participants who already had signs of cognitive decline — likely because they had more tau to clear in the first place, according to Ryman.

None of the 12 participants experienced side effects, though the protein-clearing benefits returned to baseline about an hour after the session ended. Researchers cautioned strongly against attempting the technique at home. "Breathing higher concentrations of carbon dioxide outside of these controlled settings can be dangerous and, in some cases, life-threatening," Ryman said.

Copper Drug Repairs Brain's Waste-Removal Pumps

In the second study, researchers at the University of Melbourne and Monash University targeted the problem from a different angle. Their work focused on P-glycoprotein, a transport protein embedded in the blood-brain barrier that acts as a cellular pump, grabbing amyloid-beta and pushing it out of the central nervous system.

In Alzheimer's patients, the abundance of these pumps decreases significantly, leaving the brain unable to effectively remove toxic proteins. The research team, led by Ashley Bush at the University of Melbourne, administered a copper-carrying compound called Cu(ATSM) to genetically modified mice that overproduce human amyloid-beta.

After 56 days of daily oral treatment, the results were striking. Treated mice showed a 24.1% increase in P-glycoprotein pump abundance, a 42% reduction in toxic amyloid-beta, and a nearly 44% improvement in spatial learning.

"By improving the pumps, the brain can finally clear out the trapped waste."

— Jae Pyun, Monash Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences

Bush noted he was surprised that "only 56 days of treatment were needed for conspicuous benefits." The compound also has anti-ferroptosis properties, meaning it may combat iron-dependent cell death that occurs in Alzheimer's-affected brains.

Implications for India's Growing Dementia Burden

The findings carry particular relevance for India, where an estimated 8.8 million people live with dementia, a number projected to nearly double by 2050 as the population ages. Alzheimer's accounts for roughly 60-70% of dementia cases. For the Indian diaspora, many of whom are primary caregivers for aging parents back home, affordable and accessible treatment options remain a pressing concern.

If the CO2 approach proves effective at scale, it could eventually be delivered via a portable device at home, according to Ryman — a prospect that could make it far more accessible than existing drug-based interventions, particularly in countries with limited specialist healthcare infrastructure.

What's Next

Both approaches face significant hurdles before reaching patients. The CO2 study involved only 12 participants, and researchers need to determine whether repeated sessions can slow Alzheimer's progression over time. Vincent Tay at Changi General Hospital in Singapore noted that further studies must explore "whether this does translate into any clinical benefit."

The copper drug, meanwhile, has only been tested in mice. "This was a study in mice, and there is a long road ahead for testing in humans," Bush cautioned. However, Cu(ATSM) has already progressed to clinical testing for Parkinson's disease and ALS, giving researchers confidence in its safety profile.

Jeff Iliff at the University of Washington pointed to the broader therapeutic potential of boosting the brain's clearance mechanisms. "Stimulating these clearance mechanisms is not specific to amyloid, but it can help clear amyloid, tau, alpha-synuclein and inflammatory molecules," he said, suggesting the approaches could benefit patients with a range of neurodegenerative conditions beyond Alzheimer's.
